---
executiveName: Alhaji Aminu Umar
title: BUILDING A SHIPPING INDUSTRY NIGERIANS CAN OWN AND COMPETE
position: 'President, Managing Director, Board Member.'
organisation: >-
  Nigerian Chamber of Shipping, International Chamber of Shipping, Sea Transport
  Services Nigeria Limited
photo: >-
  https://n0jyvquhgs2welj7.public.blob.vercel-storage.com/uploads/1790310973788-4ec47269-whatsapp-image-2026-09-24-at-9-45-07-pm.webp
initials: AAU
excerpt: >-
  Nigeria has one of Africa’s largest maritime markets, a significant cargo base
  and an economy that depends heavily on shipping. Yet the ability to own,
  finance, operate and manage the vessels that serve this market remains a major
  challenge for indigenous operators.
date: '2026-09-25'
transcriptRef: EC-2026-010
qa:
  - question: >-
      Why does Nigeria still import much of the maritime capability it needs,
      despite its significant cargo base, coastline and maritime market? What
      are the fundamental gaps preventing Nigeria from converting this demand
      into sustainable indigenous shipping capacity and ownership?
    answer: >-
      <p class="MsoNormal"><span style="font-weight: bolder;">Alhaji Aminu
      Umar</span><br>Thank you for having me.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">We have to accept and acknowledge that we have a
      capability

      gap in terms of the percentage of Nigerians having the opportunity or
      assets

      that are required for providing the services within the industry or the
      market

      that requires it.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, I think we accept and acknowledge that this gap
      is

      there.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">The reason why we have always been part of the
      advocacy that

      we have been pushing forward is that one of our biggest challenges in
      acquiring

      those assets is <b>access to capital</b>.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">It is not very easy to access the capital that is
      required

      for such kind of investment because, as I am sure you know, shipping
      assets are

      very highly priced.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Because they are highly priced, it is not easy to
      secure the

      capital. Even if you see the availability of capital, the cost of the
      capital

      is super high, which makes you totally uncompetitive.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">It is not comparable to what is obtainable in other
      parts of

      the globe where they are having access to capital and the cost is very
      cheap.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, we have not been able to secure or get to that
      level

      yet. This is the reason why you see this gap and, so far, it has not been
      able

      to be covered.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">On addressing the capability gap, I think number one
      is to

      have government come in to help us with access to capital.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I think in the cabotage space or trade now, the
      government

      has taken the initiative of CVFF. The President has given the directive
      and the

      Minister has confirmed the directive.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">The moment that fund is able to reach the right
      applicants,

      I am sure we will see in the cabotage market that there will be more

      participation of Nigerians in that space.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, we believe that not only the cabotage market
      should be

      getting that intervention. We also hope to see similar intervention or any
      kind

      of scheme that will help where Nigerians can be able to participate in the

      global shipping business.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">We can take a leaf from advanced countries such as
      the USA

      that have similar kinds of schemes, and China also has similar kinds of

      schemes, where they help their local entrepreneurs or shipowners with
      access to

      capital that they can be able to invest and do global
      trade.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I think we can take a leaf from what they have been
      doing

      there.<o:p></o:p></p>
  - question: >-
      Major cargo owners, including the Dangote Group, generate the kind of
      predictable demand that can support vessel investment. How important are
      long-term Contracts of Affreightment to fleet development, and what needs
      to change in the relationship between major cargo owners and indigenous
      shipowners?
    answer: >-
      <p class="MsoNormal"><b>Alhaji Aminu Umar</b></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I think on this one you have already captured
      it.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">What all financiers want to see as part of the
      document to

      be able to give you access to capital is that you have a contract that
      covers

      the time he will completely collect his funds back.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">This is long-term contracts for shipping because,
      like I

      said, they are very highly capital intensive.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Companies like Dangote, which we thank him for
      bringing this

      opportunity in Nigeria, where today we see cargoes originating from his

      refinery to all over the world, not only in Nigeria but in West Africa,
      the

      African continent or the entire globe.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I think if Dangote and any other major cargo owners
      are open

      to signing long-term contracts, it will help the Nigerian shipowners in

      particular to be able to have access to capital and be able to provide
      them

      with the required assets they need.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">This is a win-win situation for both the Nigerian
      shipowner

      as well as the cargo owner, which includes Dangote
      Refinery.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Because if you have the Nigerian shipowners here, the

      pricing for freight will be less expensive compared to the present ships
      being

      used that are internationally owned because they would have added their

      premium, they will add their war risk insurance on top of it, and that
      will

      increase their freight rate per tonne.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, if they are able to unlock this, I am sure that
      they

      will see a drop in their freight, and that will be a win-win situation for
      them

      as well as for the economy of Nigeria.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <div class="MsoNormal" align="center" style="text-align:center">


      <hr size="2" width="100%" align="center">


      </div>
  - question: >-
      You have described financing as one of the biggest challenges facing
      Nigerian shipowners. What is preventing commercial banks and other
      financial institutions from developing greater confidence and technical
      understanding of shipping, and what would make vessel financing more
      commercially viable?
    answer: >-
      <p class="MsoNormal"><b>Alhaji Aminu Umar</b></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I think, one, the banks have to first of all
      understand this

      business.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I think there is a need for the banks to invest in
      creating

      the know-how and seeing it as part of their business unit that they can
      develop

      as a product.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Presently, we have very few, if any, that understand
      the

      business as compared to international banks which are operating in Europe,
      USA

      or Asia, who have very huge departments or divisions for ship finance only

      because they have invested in creating the know-how.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">With the knowledge and resources to understand how it
      works,

      they are able to create the product that matches what the market
      needs.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, I think one is the bank to create that know-how
      and

      create the package and possibly secure where they can secure those kinds
      of

      financing to be able to give it out to potential
      shipowners.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I think this is the major thing that is creating a

      bottleneck.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">They have to look at their structure to be comparable
      to

      elsewhere in the world because if the financing is far better in Europe
      and far

      better in Asia and we are not competitive, there is no way.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Remember, the market is global.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal"><b>Shipping market is global.</b><o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">International shipowners have their capital cost low.
      Their

      principal capex at the end of the day is low. They are able to give better

      pricing.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">The cargo owner will go for the freight that is less.
      He

      will not decide based on the fact that he likes you.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">He will not decide to take a freight that will add to
      his

      cost of goods and say, you take it because I like you, when the other
      person is

      giving him a lesser freight which will give him a better return on his

      business.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, the banks must have to look at the products that
      are

      being given all across the globe and be able to say, we can match whatever
      is

      given in Asia and Europe. We can also match it here.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, if they are unable to match, then it will be
      difficult

      to have Nigerian shipowners venture into it and take the loan at whatever
      cost,

      then come into the market and say they can compete with a person who gets
      his

      own capital at a very low cost.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">It will be very difficult for the Nigerian to
      survive.<o:p></o:p></p>
  - question: >-
      The capital requirements for some major cargo opportunities can far exceed
      the capacity of existing financing instruments. What should the next
      generation of Nigeria’s maritime financing architecture look like if the
      objective is to build commercially sustainable fleets rather than simply
      finance individual vessels?
    answer: >-
      <p class="MsoNormal"><b>Alhaji Aminu Umar</b></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Well, I think since we commenced this conversation,
      we have

      looked at it from debt financing. I think we should look at other
      opportunities

      in financing.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So far, in Nigeria particularly or Africa, we have
      not

      matured enough in our market of shipping to go to or source the capital
      from

      the capital market.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, we believe the next generation should be able to
      grow or

      take it from where our generation has been able to reach and now explore
      the

      opportunities in the capital market, where you will have a very huge
      capital

      access and less cost.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Presently, most of the shipping companies have not
      been able

      to structure properly to be able to access funds from the capital market
      that

      is available in Nigeria and the African continent as a
      whole.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I think the next one, we have seen that happen in
      America,

      Europe and Asia. That is where global international shipping is
      going.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">They access funds from the capital market either
      through

      share investment or through bond market, which so far very few companies
      have

      that capability or structure to be able to access.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, we think the next generation should explore those

      opportunities, which I am sure will avail to them as the capital market is
      also

      maturing more and expanding.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <span
      style="font-size:12.0pt;line-height:115%;font-family:&quot;Calibri&quot;,sans-serif;

      mso-ascii-theme-font:minor-latin;mso-fareast-font-family:Calibri;mso-fareast-theme-font:

      minor-latin;mso-hansi-theme-font:minor-latin;mso-bidi-font-family:&quot;Times
      New Roman&quot;;

      mso-bidi-theme-font:minor-bidi;mso-ansi-language:EN-GB;mso-fareast-language:

      EN-US;mso-bidi-language:AR-SA">I think that there is a likelihood that in
      a few

      years from now, a lot of local shipping companies will access their funds
      from

      the capital market instead of going through bank finance we are doing
      today.</span>
  - question: >-
      You have recently highlighted Nigeria’s maritime data gaps. What data
      infrastructure does the industry need to support better investment and
      policy decisions, and how should Nigeria strengthen the technical and
      human capability required across ship management, marine engineering,
      shipbuilding, repair and maritime operations?
    answer: >-
      <p class="MsoNormal"><b>Alhaji Aminu Umar</b></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I will take first the maritime data, which I had made
      a

      statement relating to it at an event.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I think everyone in the industry has realised it and
      has

      seen the gap many years ago, particularly the access to data and long-term
      data

      that we can be able to review to see what are the seasonal changes in
      terms of

      cargo requirement or in terms of ship requirement in the
      country.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">We realised that there is no data that is there to
      access.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Yes, there are organisations that take records, but
      no one

      has been able to put it together as data and is able to look at
      it.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I can testify to that because we have tried
      individually as

      a company to invest, look at it and put our resources and try to do it,
      but it

      is more of an individual company doing it.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">We think that there is a high need and this is why I
      support

      the initiative of the Director General of NIMASA for trying to create that

      maritime technology innovation incubation scheme.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I have undertaken that if anybody is looking at
      investing in

      this maritime data, we are ready to work with them and we will look at
      even

      investing in it because it is something that I am very passionate
      about.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I would love to see some of this young generation
      look into

      that data. We do not mind to sit with them and guide them on how they can
      get

      it together and be able to bring out the good information that is
      required.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">We will work with them on that.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Really, we do not have any organisation that is
      keeping

      those records. Maybe they have them and are recording them somewhere, but

      nobody is having that data to say, like, we take a year now or take a

      twelve-month period and say, what are the shipping
      requirements?<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">What are the cargoes that come out of Nigeria? What
      are the

      cargoes that are coming into Nigeria at a particular month? During the dry

      season, what is coming more? What is coming less?<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">During the rainy season, what is coming in more? What
      is

      coming in less?<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">What are the percentage kind of vessels that are
      coming into

      the country in every month?<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">We can go back many years and say we have seen this.
      This is

      how the trend happened and because of that there is a change in the volume
      of

      vessels and activities that come in at this time and go out at this
      time.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I think this is something we are not able to get,
      this

      analytics and interpretation or analysis.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, we look forward to the next generation. We
      encourage

      them to look into it and it is going to become something that is sought
      after

      across the globe for decision making, not only for shipowners but for
      cargo

      owners, potential traders, even financiers who are looking at
      it.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">They will want to know.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <span
      style="font-size:12.0pt;line-height:115%;font-family:&quot;Calibri&quot;,sans-serif;

      mso-ascii-theme-font:minor-latin;mso-fareast-font-family:Calibri;mso-fareast-theme-font:

      minor-latin;mso-hansi-theme-font:minor-latin;mso-bidi-font-family:&quot;Times
      New Roman&quot;;

      mso-bidi-theme-font:minor-bidi;mso-ansi-language:EN-GB;mso-fareast-language:

      EN-US;mso-bidi-language:AR-SA">So, this is on the data
      analytics.<br><br><p class="MsoNormal"><b>BUILDING THE NEXT GENERATION OF
      MARITIME TALENT<o:p></o:p></b></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">On the capacity development and technological aspect,
      I

      think government has a huge role to play.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I think this is where we again say a big kudos to
      NIMASA,

      who has always been investing in the human capacity, particularly for

      seafarers.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">But I think it is high time that we, together, the
      industry,

      NIMASA, the regulator and government collaborate in such a way that it is
      not

      only the classroom training that is being provided, but the industry needs
      to

      collaborate with them in order to give on-the-job training.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Because we are seeing a lot of seafarer gap where we
      do not

      have this human capital availability across the globe.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">And we think it is not only for developing a Nigerian

      shipping industry.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">We believe that Nigerians, particularly the young

      generation, can access a lot of jobs across the globe because there is
      huge

      requirement for this job or career and we have so many men and women in
      Nigeria

      that are very open to going into this career.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, what we need is to recreate, among the things
      launched

      by NIMASA, which we discussed about the maritime data, is also this
      mentorship

      and human capital training.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I also made a statement to the DG that this is
      something

      that is very key and I think we in this industry will surely work with him
      on

      this.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I believe there is a lot of potential for this thing
      to

      connect the entire globe to young Nigerians going to work across the
      globe.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">But also, like you said, that will now give us the
      real

      number who will come back and develop the different segments of the
      shipping

      sector, including the development of shipbuilding, ship repair yards,

      maintenance and also operating the ships.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">This is number one. They need to operate to
      understand and

      they will now know how to repair and build the ship.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">It is a good scheme that is coming up and this is to
      confirm

      to the DG that we will key into it.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">The workforce that we need, we need him to invite the

      operators in the industry so we can work together to create it, so that
      the

      young Nigerians that are coming out are fit for the purpose that they are

      coming out to do.<o:p></o:p></p></span>
  - question: >-
      From your position within both the Nigerian and international shipping
      community, the lifting of the United States’ 12-year Condition of Entry
      restrictions on vessels arriving from Nigeria presents an important
      opportunity for the country’s maritime industry. What does this
      development mean for Nigerian shipping companies seeking greater
      international market access, and what must indigenous operators do to
      translate it into stronger shipping connectivity, trade opportunities and
      global competitiveness?
    answer: >-
      <p class="MsoNormal"><b>Alhaji Aminu Umar<o:p></o:p></b></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">First, it is a very big achievement by the Honourable

      Minister of Marine and Blue Economy.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I congratulate him on behalf of the Nigerian Chamber
      of

      Shipping as well as the Board and Council of the International Chamber of

      Shipping for achieving this great feat.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I think it is something we should all
      celebrate.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">This lifting is more like a check by the USA. It is
      not only

      that it is affecting Nigerian-owned or Nigerian-flag vessels. No. It
      affects

      any vessel that is originating from Nigeria.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, even if you are an international owner who loads
      a cargo

      from Nigeria or your last point of call is Nigeria, the moment you arrive
      at

      the shores of the United States, you must be subjected to some security
      checks.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I want to inform you what it means.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">You are going to wait and then wait for the security
      checks.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">In shipping terms, it means between you and the
      person who

      hires you, that is the charterer, who will now place you under
      off-hire.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">This means you are not on hire yet. You are losing
      money.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, in shipping terms, when somebody says you are
      waiting,

      you are losing money. Nobody will pay for whatever cost you are
      incurring.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Nobody pays until the United States Coast Guard comes

      onboard your ship, does their checks and, if they check and they are okay,
      then

      you are back on hire.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">More or less, you tender your notice of readiness and
      then

      you can now start before the port can now reschedule you to
      berth.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, if the Coast Guard has any reason not to give you
      the

      approval, then you are off-hire until you get their
      approval.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, it is a loss that owners incur.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">This is causing a lot of financial losses to ship and
      cargo

      owners, and it is creating so much fight between the ship and cargo owners

      because that creates a lot of conflict.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, this is a very huge achievement that the Minister
      and

      his team were able to get us out of.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">You will now see a lot of shipowners, whether
      Nigerians or

      global shipowners, will not mind to make a port call in Nigeria before
      going to

      the United States.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Before, even if they were scheduling the voyage, they
      made

      sure they did not come to Nigeria before going to the United States, so
      they

      would have created a diversion that would avoid Nigeria
      first.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Which will cost them in bunkers or even make Nigeria
      lose a

      lot of money because this opportunity will not come. The potential
      businesses

      it will bring.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, it is a great achievement and we look forward to
      more

      from the Minister to better shipping business in Nigeria.<o:p></o:p></p>
  - question: >-
      If Nigeria is serious about moving from a major maritime market to a
      country that owns and controls significantly more of the capability behind
      that market, what are the most critical changes that must happen now, and
      where should the responsibility for delivering them sit?
    answer: >-
      <p class="MsoNormal"><b>Alhaji Aminu Umar</b></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I think a lot of few things need to be put in
      place.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">One is to discuss how we can have access to capital
      and

      bring down cost of capital.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Two is to see how we can create human capacity
      building to

      build this capacity, because we need the seafarers.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">If we are investing in ships, the ships need to grow,
      the

      people that need to work on the ships, not only the ships but also work in
      the

      offices.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Because the people who are going to work in the
      offices are

      people who have worked on the ships who now are able to man the offices
      and

      supervise and manage those shipping businesses.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Number three is for us in these cargo opportunities
      we have

      advocated for.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Number one, the Cabotage Act needs to be implemented
      and the

      implementation of the Cabotage Act needs to follow the main purpose of the

      Cabotage Act, which is to support indigenous shipowners.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, the implementation of the Cabotage law or Act
      should

      reflect what it is made for, which is to support the Nigerian shipowners,
      not

      that cabotage should be put in the same basket with international
      shipowners.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">The Cabotage law has to be
      implemented.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">In one of the forums I discussed this.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">When you see what the developed nations have done in
      order

      to develop their shipping capacity, it is because they are implementing
      their

      own cabotage law with all strictness.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">We have seen it in China, Europe, in the
      Mediterranean,

      which is Turkey, the Black Sea. There is no waiver at all for a
      non-indigenous

      shipping company to operate in these countries.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Whatever they can do to support the local is what
      they do.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">And this is what we have seen in all Asian countries,
      all

      Mediterranean countries, all European countries as well as in the United

      States.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, this has to be done. It has to be deliberate and
      it has

      to be done properly and it has to be done to support the local shipping

      industry.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">Two is the cargo reservation.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">There should be an encouragement for all cargoes that
      are

      meant for or in the control of government to be taken by a Nigerian local

      company.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">That is what every other country is
      doing.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">We are not the first. Go to China. Every cargo that
      is meant

      or related to the Chinese government or funded by the Chinese government
      or

      supported by the Chinese government can only be transported by a Chinese

      shipping company.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">China is number two in the world. If they can do
      that, go to

      Gulf countries, Saudi, Kuwait, UAE, USA. That is what is
      done.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">So, Nigeria has to apply that to our industry because
      that

      is what needs to be done to support the local industry to be able to
      grow.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">If we want to be like China, USA, we will have to do
      what

      they are doing.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">I will encourage our leaders and regulators to look
      at what

      is done elsewhere.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal">We have the Cabotage law that is existing. We should
      follow

      it to the letter.<o:p></o:p></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal"><b>“PROMOTE, PROTECT AND PROVIDE”<o:p></o:p></b></p>


      <p class="MsoNormal"><b>“In short, the Cabotage law says PROMOTE, PROTECT
      AND

      PROVIDE for local shipping companies.”</b><o:p></o:p></p>
status: published
introduction: >-
  <p class="MsoNormal">Nigeria has one of Africa’s largest maritime markets, a

  significant cargo base and an economy that depends heavily on shipping. Yet
  the

  ability to own, finance, operate and manage the vessels that serve this market

  remains a major challenge for indigenous operators.<o:p></o:p></p><p
  class="MsoNormal"><!--[if gte vml 1]><v:shapetype

    o:title=""/>

  src="data:image/jpeg;base64,"
  v:shapes="Picture_x0020_1"><!--[endif]--><br>

  For <b>Alhaji Aminu Umar</b>, the issue is not simply whether Nigeria has

  cargo. It is whether the country can build the financial, institutional,

  technical and human capacity required to participate more meaningfully in the

  shipping value chain.<o:p></o:p></p><p class="MsoNormal">In this Executive
  Conversation with PrimeAxis, Umar

  discusses the cost of capital, the importance of long-term cargo commitments,

  the role of commercial banks, the future of maritime finance, Nigeria’s

  maritime data gap and human capacity development.<o:p></o:p></p><p
  class="MsoNormal">He also examines the significance of the lifting of the

  United States’ 12-year <b>Condition of Entry</b> restrictions on vessels

  arriving from Nigeria, a development he describes as a major achievement for

  Nigeria’s maritime industry.<o:p></o:p></p><p class="MsoNormal">








  </p><p class="MsoNormal">Umar also addresses what government, regulators,
  cargo

  owners, financial institutions and indigenous shipowners must do to create a

  stronger Nigerian shipping industry capable of participating more effectively

  in both domestic and global markets.<o:p></o:p></p>
pullQuote: One of our biggest challenges in acquiring those assets is access to capital.
closingQuote: >-
  This lifting is more like a check by the USA. It is not only that it is
  affecting Nigerian-owned or Nigerian-flag vessels. No. It affects any vessel
  that is originating from Nigeria.
editorsNote: >-
  <div class="MsoNormal" align="center" style="text-align:center">


  <hr size="2" width="100%" align="center">


  </div>


  <p class="MsoNormal"><b>EDITOR’S NOTE<o:p></o:p></b></p>


  <p class="MsoNormal">Nigeria’s shipping challenge is not simply a question of

  cargo availability. It is a question of whether the country can build the

  financial, institutional, technical and human capacity required to own and

  compete within the market that its cargo creates.<o:p></o:p></p>


  <p class="MsoNormal">In this conversation, Aminu Umar argues for a more

  deliberate approach to indigenous shipping, from access to affordable capital

  and long-term cargo commitments to stronger maritime data, practical human

  capacity development and firm implementation of the Cabotage
  framework.<o:p></o:p></p>


  <p class="MsoNormal">His central argument is ultimately about moving beyond

  participation to ownership and building companies capable of competing beyond

  Nigeria.<o:p></o:p></p>

  economy ecosystem.<o:p></o:p></p>


  <p class="MsoNormal">PrimeAxis describes the platform as a space for dialogue
